mainTopic: Why the seller swears in a disputed slave or field sale (רבי הושעיא's זוקקין vs. רב ששת's רבי מאיר reading), סומכוס on dividing money in doubt, and the new משנה on olive trees sold for wood.
overview: The משנה rules that in a disputed sale of a slave or a field, the seller takes an oath, and the גמרא works hard to explain why. A garment explanation runs into the rule that admitting a different item is not a partial admission. רב פפא answers that the garment is made of attached pieces. רבי הושעיא explains the case as a slave claimed with his clothing, or a field with its sheaves, so the oath on the movables binds an oath on the slave or field. רב ששת objects that this binding (זוקקין) is already taught elsewhere. He says instead that the משנה follows רבי מאיר, for whom a slave is like movables, and he defends this with רבן גמליאל, רבא's case of a damaged slave or field, and רבה בר אבוה's reversed version of a משנה. But a משנה about loaded vines shows that רבי מאיר agrees land gets no oath, so the גמרא returns to רבי הושעיא and explains why זוקקין needed to be taught here. Next, a ברייתא about a cow or maidservant that gave birth is tied to סומכוס, who splits money in doubt, and סומכוס is shown to agree that a Torah oath comes before splitting. Finally, a new משנה about olive trees sold for wood rules by how much oil the olives yield, and the גמרא explains that this applies when the seller gave no time for cutting.

steps.title: A garment claim does not fit the rule of partial admission
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to שמואל's garment explanation: what was claimed was not admitted, and what was admitted was not claimed.
steps.simpleTranslation: A garment? What the buyer claimed, the seller did not admit to, and what the seller admitted to, the buyer did not claim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's idea that the oath in the משנה comes from a dispute over a garment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath of מודה במקצת applies only when the defendant admits part of the exact thing claimed. If the buyer claims a large garment and the seller admits only a small one, the seller has admitted a different item. So there should be no oath at all.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits part of a claim and must take an oath on the rest

steps.confusionAlert: The objection is not that the seller denies everything. He does admit something, but it is a different item from what was claimed, so it does not count as a partial admission.

phrases.english: A garment?
What he claimed from him, he did not admit to him,
and what he admitted to him, he did not claim from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַה שֶּׁטְּעָנוֹ לֹא הוֹדָה לוֹ, וּמַה שֶּׁהוֹדָה לוֹ לֹא טְעָנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's garment explanation from the earlier part of the sugya.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's explanation that the oath in the משנה comes from a garment dispute.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Admitting a different item from the one claimed is not מודה במקצת, so no oath should apply.

steps.title: The garment is made of attached pieces
steps.stepSummary: Following רב פפא, the garment is one item sewn from pieces, so the admission is part of the same item.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב פפא said, the case is about attached pieces. Here too, the case is about attached pieces.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection by borrowing רב פפא's explanation that the garment is made of several pieces joined together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the garment is built from attached pieces, the buyer claims the whole thing and the seller admits to only some of the pieces. That is a real partial admission of the same item, so the oath works.

keyTerms.meaning: Pieces that are attached or joined together

phrases.english: As רב פפא said: with attached pieces,
here too, with attached pieces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case so the admission is part of the same item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The large and small garments seemed to be two completely different items.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is one garment made of pieces, so admitting some of the pieces is a true partial admission.

steps.title: The משנה speaks about a slave, not a garment
steps.stepSummary: רבי הושעיא objects that the משנה's wording is about a slave, so it cannot be explained as a garment case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי הושעיא found this difficult: Does the משנה say "garment"? It says "slave"!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי הושעיא attacks שמואל's explanation from the wording of the משנה itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה describes a dispute over a large or small slave. Turning it into a garment case does not match what the משנה actually says.

keyTerms.meaning: Does it teach...? (meaning: it does not)

phrases.english: It was difficult for רבי הושעיא:
Does it teach "garment"?
It teaches "slave"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the garment explanation from a new angle: the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording of the משנה is about a slave, not a garment.

steps.title: A slave with his clothing, or a field with its sheaves
steps.stepSummary: רבי הושעיא explains that the claim included both the slave and his clothing, or a field and its sheaves, so the oath on the movables brings an oath on the rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי הושעיא said: for example, where he claimed a slave together with his clothing, and a field together with its sheaves.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי הושעיא gives his own explanation of the משנה, which keeps the slave in the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally no oath is taken over a slave or land. But when the claim also includes movables, like clothing or sheaves, the oath owed on them can pull in an oath on the slave or field too. This binding is called זקיקה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explanation keeps the slave as the subject of the משנה while giving a real reason for the oath. It also sets up רב ששת's objection in step 7.

phrases.english: Rather, רבי הושעיא said:
For example, where he claimed a slave with his clothing
and a field with its sheaves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the explanation rejected in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New case definition that keeps the slave and adds movables.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה had to be about a garment alone in order to have an oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: The claim covers a slave plus his clothing (or a field plus its sheaves), and the oath on the movables binds an oath on the slave or field.

steps.title: The garment problem still remains
steps.stepSummary: Even in רבי הושעיא's case, the dispute over the clothing has the same flaw: the admission is not of what was claimed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But still, a garment: what he claimed, he did not admit to, and what he admitted to, he did not claim!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back the objection from step 1, now aimed at רבי הושעיא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי הושעיא's case needs a real oath on the clothing. But if the seller admits a different garment from the one claimed, that is still not מודה במקצת. Without an oath on the clothing, nothing binds the slave.

phrases.english: But still, a garment:
what he claimed from him, he did not admit to him,
and what he admitted to him, he did not claim from him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 4 with the same reasoning used in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The oath on the clothing in רבי הושעיא's case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Admitting a different garment is not a partial admission, so there is no oath on the clothing to bind the slave.

steps.title: Again, the garment is made of attached pieces
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the clothing is made of attached pieces, so the admission is part of the claimed garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: with attached pieces.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא solves the problem again with the same idea of a garment made of joined pieces.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the clothing is one item made of attached pieces, the seller admits part of the very garment claimed. That creates a real oath on the clothing, which can then bind the slave or field.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule of דלייפי makes a garment dispute into a true partial admission. It supports both שמואל's explanation and רבי הושעיא's.

phrases.english: רב פפא said: with attached pieces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the clothing as one garment made of pieces.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clothing admitted to was a different item from the clothing claimed.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is the same garment, partly admitted, so there is an oath that can bind the slave.

steps.title: The rule of binding is already taught elsewhere
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת objects that the law of זקיקה is already in another משנה, so our משנה would be repeating it for no reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת found this difficult: Did the משנה come to teach us binding? We already learned: property that does not serve as a guarantee binds property that does serve as a guarantee, to take an oath on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת challenges רבי הושעיא's explanation by showing that it would make our משנה repeat a law that is already known.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Movable property is "property without a guarantee," and land is "property with a guarantee." Another משנה already teaches that an oath on movables can pull in an oath on land. So if our משנה only teaches זקיקה, it adds nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: They bind (pull in an oath on other property)
Did it come to teach us?
Movable property, which does not serve as a guarantee for debts
Land, which serves as a guarantee for debts

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two kinds of property. "Without a guarantee" means movables, and "with a guarantee" means land. The movables are what bind the land.

phrases.english: It was difficult for רב ששת:
Did it come to teach us binding?!
We already learned:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in קידושין 26a.

phrases.english: Property that does not serve as a guarantee binds
the property that does serve as a guarantee
to take an oath on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ לְרַב שֵׁשֶׁת: זוֹקְקִין אֲתָא לְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the garment problem is solved, raises a new objection against רבי הושעיא's whole explanation.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי הושעיא's explanation that the משנה is about זקיקה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The law of זקיקה is already stated in the משנה in קידושין, so our משנה would be repeating it for no reason.

steps.title: רב ששת: The משנה follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the משנה follows רבי מאיר, who holds that a slave is like movable property. So an oath applies even when the dispute is over the slave alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב ששת said: Whose view is this משנה? It is רבי מאיר, who said that a slave is treated like movable property.
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected רבי הושעיא's approach, רב ששת offers his own explanation of the משנה. He says the משנה follows רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally oaths are not imposed on claims about land, and slaves are often compared to land. רבי מאיר disagrees and treats a slave like movables. So according to him, an oath can be required even when the dispute is only about the slave, and there is no need to add clothing or sheaves.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose opinion is this? (asking which תנא the משנה follows)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the new foundation for the rest of the sugya. Every challenge that follows tests whether this רבי מאיר reading can hold up.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Sheshet said:
Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Meir,
who said: a slave is like movable property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: הָא מַנִּי – רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After objecting to רבי הושעיא in step 7, רב ששת replaces that approach with his own.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the משנה to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה had to include clothing or sheaves to explain why there is an oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה follows רבי מאיר, for whom a slave alone can carry an oath because he is like movables.

steps.title: The admission does not match the claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that even under רבי מאיר, the seller admitted to a different slave than the one claimed, so there should be no oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is still a problem: what the buyer claimed, the seller did not admit, and what the seller admitted, the buyer did not claim!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב ששת's explanation. The buyer claims a big slave, and the seller admits only to a small slave, which is a different item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath for partial admission requires admitting part of what was actually claimed. Here the seller admits a different item entirely, the small slave. So it looks like a full denial of the claim, which brings no oath.

keyTerms.meaning: but still, there is still a problem

phrases.english: But still:
what he claimed from him, he did not admit to him,
and what he admitted to him, he had not claimed!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַכַּתִּי: מַה שֶּׁטְּעָנוֹ – לֹא הוֹדָה לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This attacks רב ששת's explanation from step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim that the משנה's oath works under רבי מאיר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A partial-admission oath needs an admission to part of the claim. Admitting a different slave is not part of the claim.

steps.title: The משנה follows רבן גמליאל's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה also holds like רבן גמליאל, who requires an oath even when the admission is a different item than the one claimed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה holds like רבן גמליאל. As we learned: If someone claimed wheat and the other admitted to owing barley, he is exempt from an oath, but רבן גמליאל holds him liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the משנה follows רבן גמליאל. In the wheat-and-barley case, he requires an oath even though the admission is a different item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים say that admitting barley when wheat was claimed is not a partial admission. רבן גמליאל says it still brings an oath. If our משנה agrees with רבן גמליאל, admitting the small slave when the big one was claimed can also bring an oath.

phrases.english: He holds like Rabban Gamliel.
As we learned in a משנה:
If he claimed wheat and he admitted barley, he is exempt;
Rabban Gamliel holds him liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers the challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the משנה to an additional opinion (רבן גמליאל)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Admitting a different item can never count as a partial admission.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבן גמליאל, admitting a different item still brings an oath, and our משנה follows him.

steps.title: The small slave is a case of "here you are"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the small slave is standing right there to be taken, so admitting him is הילך, which does not bring an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is still a problem: it is a case of "here, take it" (הילך)!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises another challenge to רב ששת. The small slave the seller admits to is right in front of the buyer, ready to take.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the admitted item is handed over on the spot (הילך), it is treated as if the debt was already paid. Then what remains is a full denial, which brings no oath. So even with רבן גמליאל, the oath should fall away.

keyTerms.meaning: "here you are": the admitted item is right here to take, so it does not count as an admitted debt

steps.confusionAlert: Don't confuse this with step 9. Step 9 asked whether a different item can count as an admission. This step asks whether an item that is right there to take counts as an admitted debt at all.

phrases.english: Still, it is a case of "here you are"!
phrases.notes: The small slave is standing right there, so the seller isn't really admitting a debt. He's just handing over what's already there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This raises a new problem with רב ששת's reading, even after step 10's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The oath in the משנה under רב ששת's explanation
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An admission of an item that is right there (הילך) does not count, so the claim becomes a full denial with no oath.

steps.title: רבא: The slave or field was damaged
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the seller damaged the slave or the field, so he cannot just say "here you are."
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The case is a slave whose hand the seller cut off, or a field in which the seller dug pits, ditches and caves.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the הילך challenge. In the case of the משנה, the seller damaged the slave or the field, so it is not simply sitting there ready to hand over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the seller damaged what he admitted to, he cannot just hand it over as is. He also owes for the damage. That makes his admission a real admission of a debt, not הילך, so the oath can apply.

phrases.english: Rava said:
a slave whose hand he cut off,
and a field in which he dug
pits, ditches and caves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers the הילך challenge from step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The admitted slave or field is whole and can just be handed over, which is הילך.
steps.terutzMaskana: The seller damaged it, so he cannot just hand it over, and his admission is a real admission of a debt.

steps.title: רבי מאיר seems to treat slaves like land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב ששת's basic claim: in a משנה about robbery, רבי מאיר treats slaves like land, not like movables.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we heard the opposite from רבי מאיר! As we learned: If someone robbed an animal and it aged, or slaves and they aged, he pays their value at the time of the robbery. רבי מאיר says: With slaves, he can say to the owner, "Here is yours in front of you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the foundation of רב ששת's explanation. It brings a משנה where רבי מאיר seems to treat slaves like land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A robber normally pays for any loss in value, which is the rule for movables. Land is just returned as it is, because it cannot really be stolen. רבי מאיר says aged slaves are simply returned as they are, just like land, which contradicts the claim that he treats slaves as movables.

keyTerms.meaning: according to its value at the time of the robbery
"here is yours in front of you": returning the item as is

steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge goes to the root of רב ששת's explanation. If רבי מאיר really treats slaves like land, the whole reading collapses.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר אִיפְּכָא שָׁמְעִינַן לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: But we heard the opposite from Rabbi Meir,
as we learned in a משנה:
If one robbed an animal and it aged,
or slaves, and they aged,
he pays according to the time of the robbery.
Rabbi Meir says: with slaves,
he says to him: "Here is yours in front of you"!
phrases.notes: That's the rule for land: you just give it back as it is. So רבי מאיר seems to treat slaves like land.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר אִיפְּכָא שָׁמְעִינַן לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This goes back to step 8 and challenges its basic premise about רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim that רבי מאיר holds a slave is like movables
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In robbery, רבי מאיר lets the robber return aged slaves as they are, which is the rule for land. So he seems to treat slaves like land, the opposite of what רב ששת said.

steps.title: רבה בר אבוה reverses the opinions in the robbery משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge to רב ששת. רבה בר אבוה swaps the names in the robbery משנה, so רבי מאיר holds that slaves are like movables.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is not difficult. רב ששת holds like רבה בר אבוה, who reverses the opinions and teaches: רבי מאיר says the robber pays what the slaves were worth at the time of the robbery. The חכמים say that with slaves, the robber can say to the owner, "Here is yours in front of you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 13. It cites a version of the robbery משנה in which the opinions are switched.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the usual version, רבי מאיר says "here is yours before you" for slaves, which is the rule for land. In רבה בר אבוה's version, רבי מאיר says the robber pays the value at the time of the robbery, which is the rule for movables. So רבי מאיר does treat slaves like movables, just as רב ששת claimed.

keyTerms.meaning: He reverses and teaches: he switches which opinion belongs to which Sage
The אמורא who teaches the reversed version of the משנה
According to the value at the time of the robbery, the rule for stolen movables
Here is yours before you: the robber returns the item as it is now, the rule for land

steps.confusionAlert: After the reversal, רבי מאיר is the one who says "pay as at the time of the robbery." That is the side that treats slaves like movables, which is what רב ששת needs.

phrases.english: That is not difficult,
like Rabba bar Avuh, who reverses and teaches:
phrases.notes: He switches the names of the two opinions in the robbery משנה quoted in step 13.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: מְשַׁלֵּם כִּשְׁעַת הַגְּזֵילָה,
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: he pays according to the time of the robbery,
and the Sages say:
with slaves, he says to him:
"Here is yours before you."

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא לָא קַשְׁיָא, כִּדְמַחְלֵיף רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ וְתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 13 by citing a reversed version of the robbery משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different version of the source (the opinions are swapped)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In the robbery משנה, רבי מאיר treats slaves like land, which contradicts רב ששת.
steps.terutzMaskana: In רבה בר אבוה's version, רבי מאיר treats slaves like movables, so רב ששת is supported.

steps.title: How do we know רבי מאיר compares land to a slave?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know רבי מאיר requires an oath for land. Perhaps he requires it only for a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: But from where do we know that רבי מאיר compares land to a slave, so that just as an oath is taken on a slave, an oath is also taken on land? Perhaps an oath is taken only on a slave, but not on land!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge to רב ששת's explanation of our משנה. רבי מאיר said slaves are like movables, but he never said anything about land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה also has a dispute about a small field or a big field, and an oath is taken there too. For רב ששת's explanation to work, רבי מאיר must hold that an oath is taken on land as well. The גמרא asks where we see that, since רבי מאיר may treat slaves like movables while still exempting land from an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: We compare (two things, so they share the same law)

phrases.english: But from where do we know
that Rabbi Meir holds
we compare land to a slave:
just as for a slave an oath is taken,
so too for land an oath is taken?
Perhaps it is on a slave that an oath is taken,
but on land, no!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִמַּאי דְּסָבַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר מַקְּשִׁינַן קַרְקַע לְעֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that רבי מאיר treats slaves like movables, then asks whether that rule reaches land.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's assumption that, according to רבי מאיר, an oath is taken on land as well
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Treating slaves like movables does not show that land has the same oath rule. רבי מאיר could require an oath for a slave and still exempt land.

steps.title: Introducing a ברייתא about animals and a maidservant that gave birth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that רבי מאיר separates slaves from land and begins quoting a ברייתא as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: It should not enter your mind that רבי מאיר makes this distinction, as it is taught in a ברייתא: one who trades a cow for a donkey, and the cow gave birth; and similarly, one who sells his maidservant, and she gave birth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer by quoting a ברייתא. This part only sets up the cases. The rulings and the proof come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes two sales in which a baby was born, and no one knows whether it was born before or after the sale. One case involves an animal and one involves a maidservant. The rulings that follow will show how רבי מאיר treats slaves and land.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not enter your mind: that idea is wrong
One who exchanges (trades one item for another)

phrases.english: It should not enter your mind,
as it is taught in a baraita:
one who exchanges a cow for a donkey, and it gave birth,
and similarly one who sells his maidservant, and she gave birth,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the answer to the challenge in step 15 by bringing a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי מאיר does not separate slaves from land when it comes to an oath
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a traded cow and a sold maidservant that gave birth

steps.title: Seller claims the birth, buyer is silent
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's first ruling: if the seller says the birth happened while he still owned the mother, and the buyer says nothing, the seller wins.
steps.simpleTranslation: If this one (the seller) says, "It was born while still in my possession," and that one (the buyer) stays silent, the seller is entitled to the baby.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting the ברייתא and gives its first, simple ruling. The ברייתא is not finished, and the proof for רבי מאיר comes later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the seller makes a claim, and the buyer does not argue. So the seller takes the baby. This simple case sets the stage for the harder cases where both sides make claims.

keyTerms.meaning: In my possession (the birth happened while I still owned the mother)

phrases.english: this one says: in my possession,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the seller, saying the baby was born before the sale.

phrases.english: and that one remains silent, he is entitled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from step 16 with its first ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When only the seller makes a claim and the buyer stays silent, the seller takes the baby.

steps.title: When neither side knows, they split
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's second ruling: if both seller and buyer say 'I don't know' when the birth happened, they divide the offspring.
steps.simpleTranslation: If this one says 'I don't know' and that one says 'I don't know,' they split it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the ברייתא. This is the second case: neither side knows when the birth happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither side has a stronger claim, so the value of the offspring is divided between them. This is still part of the ברייתא's background cases. The key case for the proof comes in the next line.

phrases.english: This one says: "I do not know,"
and that one says: "I do not know" —
they divide.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה אוֹמֵר: ״אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ״, וְזֶה אוֹמֵר: ״אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted in steps 16-17 with its second case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When both sides are unsure, the offspring is split.

steps.title: Both claim the birth happened in their possession
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's key case: both sides say 'in my possession.' רבי מאיר says the seller swears and keeps it. חכמים say there is no oath on slaves or land.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the seller says 'it was born while I owned the mother' and the buyer says 'it was born while I owned the mother,' the seller swears that the birth happened in his possession. This is because anyone who takes a Torah oath swears and does not pay. These are the words of רבי מאיר. חכמים say: no oath is taken on slaves or on land.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the ברייתא's last case and the heart of the proof. רבי מאיר and חכמים disagree about whether an oath is taken here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר requires an oath in a case involving a maidservant, a slave. חכמים answer that there is no oath on slaves or on land. The way חכמים mention land along with slaves is what the גמרא will try to use as proof in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: In my possession, while I owned it
They swear and do not pay

phrases.english: This one says: "In my possession,"
phrases.notes: This is the seller, saying the birth happened before he sold the mother.

phrases.english: and that one says: "In my possession" —
phrases.notes: This is the buyer, saying the birth happened after he bought her.

phrases.english: the seller swears that she gave birth in his possession,
because all who take an oath by Torah law
take the oath and do not pay,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say:
One does not take an oath, not on slaves
and not on land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא with the case that contains the מחלוקת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: the seller swears and keeps the offspring. חכמים: no oath on slaves or land.
steps.whyThisMatters: The proof that רבי מאיר requires an oath on land depends on how we read חכמים's reply here.

steps.title: Inference that רבי מאיר requires an oath on land too
steps.stepSummary: Since חכמים answered 'no oath on slaves or land,' it seems רבי מאיר holds there is an oath on both.
steps.simpleTranslation: Doesn't this show that רבי מאיר holds one does take an oath, even on land?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws its proof from the ברייתא. חכמים's reply mentions land, so it seems רבי מאיר disagrees about land too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If חכמים argue against רבי מאיר about both slaves and land, then רבי מאיר seems to require an oath on both. That would answer the question from step 15: רבי מאיר does not limit the oath to slaves.

phrases.english: Is it not by inference
that Rabbi Meir holds one takes an oath!
phrases.notes: He means an oath on both slaves and land.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָאו מִכְּלָל דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר סָבַר נִשְׁבָּעִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the proof from the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that רבי מאיר requires an oath on land, not only on slaves.
steps.raayaSupportSource: חכמים's reply in the ברייתא: 'no oath on slaves or on land.'

steps.title: Maybe חכמים meant 'just as you agree about land'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. חכמים may have said: just as you agree with us that there is no oath on land, agree about slaves too.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do you know that? Maybe they were saying to him 'just as': just as you agree with us about land, agree with us about slaves too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proof from step 20. It offers another way to read חכמים's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חכמים may have mentioned land because רבי מאיר already agrees there is no oath on land. They are pushing him to treat slaves the same way. If so, the ברייתא does not prove that רבי מאיר requires an oath on land. Steps 22-23 go on to show that he really does agree about land.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as (an argument from something already agreed)

steps.confusionAlert: Read חכמים's words in two ways. In step 20 they are disagreeing with רבי מאיר about both slaves and land. Here they agree with him about land and argue only about slaves.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא does not prove that רבי מאיר requires an oath on land. חכמים may have been building on his agreement about land.

phrases.english: From where do you know this?
Perhaps they are saying to him "just as":
just as you agree with us regarding land —
agree with us also regarding slaves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference made in step 20.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that רבי מאיר requires an oath on land.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: חכמים may have mentioned land as something רבי מאיר already agrees to, not as a point of dispute.

steps.title: Proof from the vines משנה that רבי מאיר agrees about land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה where רבי מאיר says some things are 'like land but not like land,' and requires a שבועה in a claim about ten loaded vines.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know this, as we learned in a משנה: רבי מאיר says there are things that are like land but are not treated like land, and חכמים do not agree with him. How so? Someone says, 'I handed you ten vines loaded with grapes,' and the other says, 'There were only five.' רבי מאיר requires a שבועה. חכמים say anything attached to the ground is like the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for its rejection in Step 21, that רבי מאיר agrees there is no שבועה on land. This step quotes the source. The next step explains why it proves the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר's own wording is 'things that are like land but not like land.' That implies real land has no שבועה, and only certain special items get one. The argument with חכמים is about those special items, the loaded vines.

keyTerms.meaning: Obligates, here to take a שבועה

phrases.english: Know this, as we learned:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in שבועות 42b.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
There are things that are like land
but are not treated like land.
And the Rabbis do not agree with him.
How so?
'I handed you ten loaded vines,'
and the other says: 'There were only five,'
Rabbi Meir obligates him.
phrases.notes: He has to swear, because he admitted to part of the claim.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַמְחוּבָּר לַקַּרְקַע – הֲרֵי הוּא כַּקַּרְקַע.
phrases.english: Anything attached to the ground is like the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the דחיה of Step 21 by showing רבי מאיר agrees there is no שבועה on land.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי מאיר agrees there is no שבועה on land
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in שבועות about ten loaded vines

steps.title: The argument is only about grapes ready to be picked
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא says רבי מאיר and חכמים argue only about grapes ready for harvest. That shows רבי מאיר agrees real land gets no שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: the difference between them is grapes that are ready to be picked. One master, רבי מאיר, holds they count as already picked. The other master, חכמים, holds they do not count as picked.
steps.whatsHappening: This finishes the proof. The argument in the vines משנה is narrowed down to ripe grapes only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר requires a שבועה only because he sees ripe grapes as already harvested, which makes them movable property. So for true land, even רבי מאיר agrees there is no שבועה. This supports Step 21's reading of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Grapes that are ready to be picked
This is the difference between them
They are considered as already picked

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר agrees there is no שבועה on real land. He argues only about things like ripe grapes, which he treats as already picked.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
Grapes that are ready to be picked
are the difference between them.
For one master holds: they are like already picked,
phrases.notes: The first 'master' is רבי מאיר and the second is חכמים.

phrases.english: and the other master holds: they are not like picked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה from Step 22 so it proves the point.
steps.raayaObject: רבי מאיר agrees land itself gets no שבועה
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוסי בר חנינא's narrowing of the argument to ripe grapes

steps.title: Going back to רבי הושעיא's explanation
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת's reading fails, because רבי מאיר agrees there is no oath on land, yet our משנה also has a field case. So the גמרא goes back to רבי הושעיא's explanation of our משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, really the משנה is as רבי הושעיא explained.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to an explanation from earlier in the sugya, רבי הושעיא's. This sets up the next step, which answers the problem that had been raised against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 22-23 showed that רבי מאיר agrees land gets no שבועה. Our משנה also requires an oath in a dispute over a field, so רב ששת's explanation, which rests on רבי מאיר, cannot work. רבי הושעיא's approach explains the oath through movable items (clothing, sheaves) that pull in the slave or field, so the גמרא goes back to it.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, really: going back to a position
The אמורא whose explanation was given earlier

phrases.english: Rather, really it is like Rabbi Hoshaya,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Once Step 23 shows רבי מאיר agrees about land, the גמרא goes back to רבי הושעיא's reading.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב ששת's explanation, that the משנה follows רבי מאיר and requires an oath on a slave or field alone, could stand.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה is explained as רבי הושעיא said: a slave claimed with his clothing, or a field with its sheaves.

steps.title: Why the זוקקין teaching was still needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the earlier difficulty that זוקקין is already known. Without this teaching, we might have thought a slave's garment counts as the slave, and a field's sheaves count as the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: As for the difficulty you raised about 'binding': it was needed. You might have thought a slave's garment is treated like the slave, and the sheaves of a field are treated like the field. So it teaches us they are not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem that had been raised against רבי הושעיא's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difficulty was that the rule of זוקקין is already taught elsewhere, so why repeat it here? The answer is that this case adds something new. A garment and sheaves are separate movable items, not part of the slave or land, so they can bring a שבועה. That שבועה then pulls in the slave or land with it.

keyTerms.meaning: Binding: movable property pulls land into a שבועה

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's שבועה comes from movable items, the garment and the sheaves, which pull in the slave and the field through זוקקין.

phrases.english: And what was difficult for you, 'binding'?
phrases.notes: The difficulty was that the rule of זוקקין is already taught in the משנה in קידושין.

phrases.english: It was necessary:
You might have thought to say
a slave's garment is like the slave,
the sheaves of a field are like the field,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי הושעיא's explanation, chosen in Step 24, against the earlier difficulty.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the teaching adds something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A slave's garment counts as the slave and a field's sheaves count as the field, so there is no שבועה at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are separate movable items. They bring a שבועה, and that שבועה pulls in the slave or land.

steps.title: Whose view is 'both don't know, they divide'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's ruling that if both sides say 'I don't know,' they divide. It asks whose opinion that is.
steps.simpleTranslation: If this one says 'I don't know' and that one says 'I don't know,' they divide. Whose opinion is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It goes back to another line of the ברייתא from Step 18 and asks who holds that view. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually whoever wants to take money from another must bring proof. So splitting the offspring when nobody knows the facts is unusual, and the גמרא wants to know whose opinion it follows.

phrases.english: This one says: 'I don't know,'
and that one says: 'I don't know', they divide.
Whose view is this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the שבועה question and analyzes a different clause of the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that money in doubt is divided

steps.title: It follows סומכוס: money in doubt is divided
steps.stepSummary: The ruling follows סומכוס, who holds that money whose ownership is in doubt is split between the two sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is סומכוס, who said: money whose ownership is in doubt is divided.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the 'divide it' ruling is the view of סומכוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סומכוס holds that when it is unclear who owns money, both sides split it. He does not require the claimant to bring proof. That fits the ברייתא's case where both say 'I don't know.'

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא with a known view on money in doubt
Money whose ownership is in doubt

steps.whatToRemember: The 'both don't know, divide' ruling follows סומכוס, who holds that money in doubt is split.

phrases.english: It is Sumakhos, who said:
Money that lies in doubt is divided.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ruling follows סומכוס: money in doubt is divided.

steps.title: The end of the ברייתא has the seller swear instead of splitting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the end of the ברייתא, where both sides are certain and the seller takes an oath. It asks: according to רבה בר רב הונא, who says סומכוס splits even when both sides are certain, why is there no split here?
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the end of the ברייתא: one says 'it gave birth while it was mine,' and the other says 'it gave birth while it was mine.' The seller swears and keeps the offspring. But רבה בר רב הונא says סומכוס holds you split even when both sides are sure. If so, why does the seller swear? The ruling should be 'they split'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last part of the same ברייתא and uses it to attack רבה בר רב הונא's reading of סומכוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The step before said the ברייתא follows סומכוס, who splits money when ownership is in doubt. רבה בר רב הונא holds that סומכוס splits even when each side claims to know for sure (בָּרִי וּבָרִי). But in the end of the ברייתא both sides are sure, and the ruling is an oath, not a split. So it seems סומכוס does not split in a case of certain against certain.

keyTerms.meaning: Now look at the end of the same source
In my possession; it happened while the animal was mine
Both sides claim to know for sure
It should have said; this is what we would expect

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides here say the very same word, בִּרְשׁוּתִי. The seller means 'it gave birth before I sold it,' and the buyer means 'it gave birth after I bought it.'

phrases.english: Say the latter clause:
This one says, "In my possession"
and that one says, "In my possession"
the seller takes an oath that it gave birth in his possession.
But according to רבה בר רב הונא, who says:

phrases.aramaic: אִין, אָמַר סוֹמְכוֹס אֲפִילּוּ בָּרִי וּבָרִי,
phrases.english: Yes, סומכוס said his rule even when it is certain against certain,
why does the seller take an oath?
It should have said "they divide"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא, דְּאָמַר: אִין, אָמַר סוֹמְכוֹס אֲפִילּוּ בָּרִי וּבָרִי, אַמַּאי יִשָּׁבַע מוֹכֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It challenges the claim from step 27 that the ברייתא follows סומכוס, when סומכוס is read the way רבה בר רב הונא reads him.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר רב הונא's view that סומכוס splits even in a case of certain against certain
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the end of the ברייתא both sides are certain, yet the ruling is an oath, not a split. If the ברייתא follows סומכוס, this goes against רבה בר רב הונא's reading.

steps.title: סומכוס agrees there is no split when a Torah oath applies
steps.stepSummary: סומכוס agrees that we do not split when a Torah-law oath applies. The case is one where the maidservant's hand was cut off, as in רבא's explanation, so the Torah oath really does apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: סומכוס agrees that when there is an oath from the Torah, we do not split. And the case is where he cut off her hand, as רבא explained.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבה בר רב הונא. Splitting is only the rule when no Torah oath settles the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סומכוס's splitting rule is used only when there is no other way to decide the case. A Torah-law oath is such a way, so it comes first. To show that a Torah oath truly applies here, the גמרא uses רבא's earlier setup: the seller cut off the slave's hand. Because of that, the seller cannot just say 'here, take what I admit to,' which would have cancelled the oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Agrees; admits that in this case
An oath that the Torah requires

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a limit on סומכוס: splitting does not replace a Torah-law oath.

phrases.english: סומכוס agrees
where there is an oath required by Torah law (there is no splitting),
and the case is where he cut off her hand, like רבא.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוֹדֶה סוֹמְכוֹס הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא שְׁבוּעָה דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the challenge of step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits סומכוס's rule so it does not apply when a Torah oath applies, and uses רבא's case setup
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought that if סומכוס splits even when both sides are certain, he should split in the ברייתא's last case too.
steps.terutzMaskana: A Torah-law oath comes before splitting. In רבא's case of the cut hand, the Torah oath applies, so the seller swears.
steps.whatToRemember: סומכוס's splitting rule gives way whenever a Torah-law oath can settle the case.

steps.title: New משנה: olive trees sold for wood grew only a little oil
steps.stepSummary: Someone sold olive trees to be cut down for wood, and before they were cut they grew olives. If the olives would give less than a רביעית (a quarter-לוג) of oil per סאה, the olives belong to the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone sells his olive trees for wood, and they grew olives giving less than a רביעית of oil per סאה. These olives belong to the owner of the trees.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. Its first case is about olive trees sold for their wood that grew olives giving only a small amount of oil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The trees now belong to the buyer, so anything small that grows on them is his. Olives this weak in oil are not treated as an important crop, so the seller has no claim to them.

keyTerms.meaning: His olive trees, sold to be used for wood
A quarter of a לוג, a small measure of liquid
A measure of volume, here of olives
The owner of the olive trees, meaning the buyer

phrases.english: MISHNA
One who sells his olive trees for wood,
and they produced (olives giving) less than a quarter (log of oil) per se'a,
these belong to the owner of the olive trees.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Olives giving less than a quarter-log of oil per סאה belong to the buyer of the trees.

steps.title: If the olives give a רביעית per סאה, they split
steps.stepSummary: If the olives give a רביעית of oil per סאה, the buyer says his trees grew them and the seller says his land grew them. They split the olives.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they produced a רביעית per סאה, this one says 'My trees grew them,' and that one says 'My land grew them.' They split.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives its second case: the olives are rich enough in oil to matter, and both sides have a claim to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the olives are a real crop. Both the trees, which belong to the buyer, and the land's nourishment, which belongs to the seller, helped them grow. Since each side has a fair claim, the משנה rules that they divide the olives.
steps.whatToRemember: Less than a רביעית of oil per סאה goes to the buyer. A רביעית goes to both: they split.

phrases.english: If they produced a quarter (log) per se'a,
this one says: "My olive trees grew them,"
and that one says: "My land grew them"
they divide.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָשׂוּ רְבִיעִית לַסְּאָה, זֶה אוֹמֵר: ״זֵיתַי גִּדֵּלוּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second case of the same משנה, where the olives give more oil.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Olives giving a quarter-log of oil per סאה are split between the buyer and the seller.

steps.title: A river carries olive trees into another person's field
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends with the case of olive trees swept by a river into someone else's field. The tree owner and the land owner both claim the olives, so they split them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a river swept away a person's olive trees and set them down in his friend's field, and they grew olives there, this one says: 'My olive trees grew them,' and that one says: 'My land grew them.' They split the olives.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives one more case with the same pattern as before. A river moves olive trees into another person's field, and both owners claim the olives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each side has a real claim. The trees belong to one person and the soil that fed them belongs to the other. Since neither claim beats the other, the משנה rules that they split the olives.

keyTerms.meaning: His fellow's field, someone else's land
My olive trees grew them (the tree owner's claim)
My land grew them (the land owner's claim)

steps.whatToRemember: In the river case, the trees belong to one person and the soil to another. Both helped grow the olives, so the olives are split.

phrases.english: A river swept away his olive trees
and set them down in his fellow's field,
this one says: 'My olive trees grew them,'
and that one says: 'My land grew them' –
they split.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁטַף נָהָר זֵיתָיו וּנְתָנָם לְתוֹךְ שְׂדֵה חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a parallel case to step 31: two sides each claim that their property grew the olives, and the olives are split.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a river moves one person's olive trees into another's field, the olives they grow are split between the tree owner and the land owner.

steps.title: What exactly did the seller tell the buyer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the trees sold for wood. It asks what the seller said about cutting them down. If he said 'cut now,' all the olives should go to him. If he said 'cut whenever you like,' all the olives should go to the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the case? If the seller told him 'Cut them down right away,' then even less than a quarter-measure should go to the land owner. If he told him 'Cut them down whenever you want,' then even a quarter-measure should go to the owner of the trees!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's split ruling in the sold-trees case. It shows that either possible instruction from the seller seems to give a clear answer, with no reason to split.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller said 'cut immediately,' he clearly did not want his land feeding the buyer's trees, so every olive belongs to him. If he said 'cut whenever you want,' he clearly allowed it, so every olive belongs to the buyer. Either way, the size of the crop (less than a quarter or a full quarter) should not matter.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
The owner of the land (here, the seller)
A quarter-לוג of oil per סאה of olives, the amount the משנה uses as the dividing line

steps.confusionAlert: This question is NOT about the river case that was just quoted. The גמרא is going back to the earlier case in the משנה, where olive trees were sold to be cut down for wood (steps 30-31).

phrases.english: גמרא:
What is the case?
phrases.notes: He is asking about the trees sold for wood (steps 30-31), not the river case right before this.

phrases.english: If he told him: 'Cut them down right away' –
then even less than a quarter
should also go to the owner of the land.
If he told him:
'Cut them down whenever you want' –
then even a quarter should go to the owner of the olive trees!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִי דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ קוֹץ לְאַלְתַּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the river case and returns to the sold-trees ruling in steps 30-31 to question how it works.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that the olives depend on whether there is less than a quarter or a full quarter (steps 30-31)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whatever the seller told the buyer would already decide who owns all the olives, so the quarter-measure dividing line seems pointless.

steps.title: The seller gave no time, so it depends on what people usually mind
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about a seller who just said 'cut them down' without saying when. People usually don't mind small amounts (less than a quarter), but they do mind larger amounts (a quarter).
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the rule is needed where he told him to cut them without saying when. Less than a quarter: people don't mind. A quarter: people do mind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about a third situation. The seller told the buyer to cut the trees but gave no time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With no clear instruction, we go by what people usually care about. A small yield is something sellers let go, so the buyer keeps it. A yield of a quarter is something sellers care about, so they split it, as step 31 ruled.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed for (a different case)
People mind, they are strict about it

steps.whatToRemember: The quarter-measure line only applies when the seller gave no time for cutting. Then the ruling follows what people usually mind.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that when people leave something unsaid, הלכה fills the gap by asking what ordinary people usually care about.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where he told him without saying when:
less than a quarter – people don't mind,
a quarter – people do mind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 33 by describing a third case that the question did not consider.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case: the seller gave no instruction about timing
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every case must involve a clear 'cut now' or 'cut whenever' instruction, which would make the quarter-measure meaningless.
steps.terutzMaskana: With no instruction, ordinary expectations decide. Below a quarter goes to the buyer, and a quarter is split.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן פזי begins to explain the quarter-measure
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן פזי starts to explain what the quarter-measure in the משנה means. His explanation continues on the next עמוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן פזי said: And the quarter that they mentioned –
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. רבי שמעון בן פזי is about to clarify the quarter-measure, and his explanation continues on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the quarter-measure is the dividing line, the next question is exactly what it measures. The words 'that they mentioned' point back to the רביעית in the משנה, which רבי שמעון בן פזי is about to define.

keyTerms.meaning: The quarter that they (the חכמים of the משנה) mentioned

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said:
And the quarter that they mentioned –

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי: וּרְבִיעִית שֶׁאָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 34's use of the quarter-measure and begins to define it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Opens a definition of the quarter-measure mentioned in the משנה. The definition itself continues on the next עמוד.
